In the limit where the electromagnetic field is purely static and has no magnetic component (i.e., $\mathbf{B}=0$ and $\mathbf{E}$ is time-independent), the electromagnetic field tensor $F^{\mu

This tensor encapsulates the complete description of the electromagnetic field in spacetime, demonstrating how electric and magnetic fields are intertwined aspects of a single phenomenon.

ads-cft-link-5cfb4fcf.interpretation:
In the context of the AdS/CFT correspondence, the term 
 dS^2
 represents the infinitesimal line element squared, which defines the geometry of the spacetime, particularly in anti-de Sitter space. The '\text{Emergent Quantity}' is a placeholder for a complex operator or correlation function in the conformal field theory (CFT) living on the boundary of the AdS space. The equality implies that geometric properties of the bulk spacetime, as described by its metric 
 dS^2
 , can be mapped to or derived from the dynamics and observables of the CFT. For instance, the energy-momentum tensor in the CFT corresponds to the metric perturbations in the AdS bulk, and correlation functions in the CFT can be computed using gravitational methods in AdS. This suggests a holographic principle where a lower-dimensional quantum field theory encodes all the information of a higher-dimensional gravitational theory.
ads-cft-link-5cfb4fcf.conceptual_definition:
The AdS/CFT correspondence, also known as gauge/gravity duality, is a profound conjecture in theoretical physics that proposes a duality between a quantum gravity theory in an anti-de Sitter (AdS) spacetime and a conformal field theory (CFT) living on the boundary of that spacetime. The equation 
 dS^2 = \text{Emergent Quantity}
 is a highly abstract representation of this link, where 
 dS^2
 typically denotes the spacetime metric in a curved geometry (often related to the gravitational side), and 
 \text{Emergent Quantity}
 represents a quantity arising from the strongly coupled quantum field theory on the boundary. This signifies that properties of gravity in the bulk (AdS) can be understood in terms of a quantum field theory on its boundary, and vice versa. It suggests that spacetime itself, or at least its geometric properties, can emerge from the dynamics of a quantum field theory.
ads-cft-link-5cfb4fcf.intuitive_summary: Gravity in a higher-dimensional 'bulk' spacetime is equivalent to a quantum field theory without gravity living on its lower-dimensional 'boundary'.

quantum-crowding-75f2839b.interpretation: The equation for the degeneracy pressure of a non-relativistic electron gas is given by $P_{deg} = \frac${(3\pi^2)^{2/3} \hbar^2}{5m_e} n_e^{5/3}$. Here, $P_{deg}$ represents the degeneracy pressure, measured in Pascals (Pa). The term $(3\pi^2)^{2/3}$ is a dimensionless constant arising from the integration over the Fermi sphere in momentum space. $\hbar$ is the reduced Planck constant (approximately $1.055 \times 10^{-34}$ J·s), which quantifies the fundamental discreteness of quantum mechanics. $m_e$ is the rest mass of an electron (approximately $9.109 \times 10^{-31}$ kg). The term $n_e$ is the number density of electrons, representing the number of electrons per unit volume (measured in m⁻³). The exponent $5/3$ indicates how the pressure scales with electron density in the non-relativistic regime: as the electron density increases, the degeneracy pressure increases rapidly.
quantum-crowding-75f2839b.symmetry_origin: This formula is derived from the principles of quantum mechanics and statistical mechanics, specifically the Pauli exclusion principle and the Fermi-Dirac distribution. The derivation involves considering the ground state energy of a system of non-interacting fermions confined to a volume. By integrating over the Fermi surface in momentum space and accounting for the degeneracy of quantum states, one arrives at the expression for the Fermi energy and subsequently the degeneracy pressure. The pressure is related to the energy density and is a consequence of the fermions filling up energy levels up to the Fermi energy, creating an outward pressure to counteract compression.
quantum-crowding-75f2839b.limits_and_boundary: In the limit of very low electron density $n_e \to 0$, the degeneracy pressure $P_{deg} \to 0$, as expected, since there are few particles to exert pressure. As the electron density $n_e \to \infty$, the degeneracy pressure $P_{deg} \to \infty$ according to the $n_e^{5/3}$ dependence. This formula is strictly valid for non-relativistic electrons, meaning their kinetic energy is much less than their rest mass energy. At extremely high densities, electrons become relativistic, and a different formula for degeneracy pressure, involving the speed of light, must be used.
quantum-crowding-75f2839b.conceptual_definition: The formula describes the pressure exerted by a degenerate electron gas in the non-relativistic limit. Degenerate matter arises when quantum mechanical effects become dominant due to high particle density, preventing particles from occupying the same quantum state and thus creating a pressure even at absolute zero temperature. This pressure, known as degeneracy pressure, is a fundamental concept in astrophysics, particularly for understanding white dwarf stars and neutron stars.
quantum-crowding-75f2839b.intuitive_summary: The degeneracy pressure of electrons increases significantly with their density, as quantum mechanics forces them into higher energy states when crowded.

field-potential-relation-ff253821.interpretation:
The equation $E$ = -$
abla\Phi$ - $ rac{\partial A}{\partial t}$ describes how the electric field ($E$), a vector quantity representing the force per unit charge, is related to two scalar potentials: the electric scalar potential ($Φ$) and the magnetic vector potential ($A$). The term -$
abla\Phi$ represents the contribution to the electric field arising from the spatial variation of the electric scalar potential. The gradient operator ($
abla$) signifies that the electric field points in the direction of the steepest decrease of the scalar potential, with its magnitude proportional to that rate of decrease. This part is analogous to the relationship between force and potential energy in mechanics, where force is the negative gradient of potential energy. The second term, -$ rac{\partial A}{\partial t}$, accounts for the contribution to the electric field that arises from the time-varying magnetic field, which is related to the magnetic vector potential by $\mathbf{B} = 
abla 	imes A$. Specifically, the time derivative of the magnetic vector potential directly induces an electric field. This term is crucial in understanding electromagnetic induction, as described by Faraday's law. Together, these two terms provide a complete description of the electric field in all situations, including those involving changing magnetic fields.
field-potential-relation-ff253821.symmetry_origin: This equation is derived from Maxwell's equations, specifically from Faraday's law of induction and the definition of the electric field in terms of potentials. In a static situation ($\frac{\partial A}{\partial t} = 0$), the electric field is purely derivable from the scalar potential ($E = -\nabla Φ$). However, in the presence of time-varying magnetic fields, the scalar potential alone is insufficient to describe the electric field. The introduction of the magnetic vector potential ($A$) allows for a more general formulation that is consistent with the relativistic nature of electromagnetism and gauge invariance.
field-potential-relation-ff253821.limits_and_boundary: In the limit where the magnetic vector potential is constant in time (i.e., $\frac{\partial A}{\partial t} = 0$), the equation reduces to $\mathbf{E} = -\nabla Φ$), describing the electric field in electrostatics, where the field is solely determined by the spatial distribution of the scalar potential. As the time variation of the vector potential $\frac{\partial A}{\partial t}$ approaches zero, the contribution from electromagnetic induction vanishes. Conversely, in situations with rapidly changing magnetic fields, the term $\frac{\partial A}{\partial t}$ can become significant and dominate the electric field's behavior.
field-potential-relation-ff253821.conceptual_definition: This equation establishes the fundamental relationship between the electric field ($E$) and the scalar electric potential ($Φ$) and the vector magnetic potential ($A$). It demonstrates that the electric field is not only derived from the spatial variation of the scalar potential (analogous to how a force is related to potential energy) but also from the time variation of the vector potential, which accounts for electromagnetic induction.
field-potential-relation-ff253821.intuitive_summary: The electric field is the negative gradient of the scalar potential plus the negative time rate of change of the vector potential.

intrinsic-weight-5e1302fa.interpretation: In this formula, rf is the intrinsic mass of the fundamental particle. yf represents the Yukawa coupling constant for that specific fermion, which quantifies the strength of the interaction between the fermion and the Higgs field. The term v denotes the vacuum expectation value (VEV) of the Higgs field, which is a non-zero constant value that the Higgs field settles into in the vacuum state. The formula posits that a particle's mass is directly proportional to both its coupling strength to the Higgs field and the Higgs field's VEV. The √2 factor is a convention often encountered in the derivation of these mass terms in quantum field theory.
intrinsic-weight-5e1302fa.symmetry_origin: This formula originates from the spontaneous symmetry breaking of the electroweak symmetry in the Standard Model. Initially, the fundamental particles are massless due to the symmetries of the underlying Lagrangian. However, the Higgs field has a potential that causes it to acquire a non-zero vacuum expectation value. This non-zero VEV breaks the electroweak symmetry, and the interaction terms between the fermions and the Higgs field, when expanded in terms of the Higgs field's fluctuations around its VEV, manifest as mass terms for the fermions.
intrinsic-weight-5e1302fa.limits_and_boundary: If the Yukawa coupling constant yf were zero, the intrinsic mass rf would also be zero, indicating that particles that do not interact with the Higgs field remain massless. As the Yukawa coupling constant yf or the Higgs VEV v increases, the intrinsic mass rf of the particle also increases proportionally. This formula does not have explicit boundaries in terms of yf or v approaching infinity, but in physical reality, these values are constrained by experimental observations and the consistency of the Standard Model.
intrinsic-weight-5e1302fa.conceptual_definition: The formula describes the intrinsic mass of a fundamental particle, specifically in the context of the Standard Model's Higgs mechanism. It relates the mass of a particle to the vacuum expectation value of the Higgs field and the coupling strength between the particle and the Higgs field. The factor of √2 arises from conventions in specific field theory calculations.
intrinsic-weight-5e1302fa.intuitive_summary: A particle acquires mass through its interaction with the pervasive Higgs field, with stronger interactions resulting in greater intrinsic mass.

Its value is approximately $1.22 imes 10^{19}$ GeV/c^2. In this context, $M_{Pl}^2$ represents the square of this fundamental mass relevant to quantum gravity in 4 spacetime dimensions.

curled-dimensions-ec181bd3.interpretation: This equation is a key relationship in theories of extra dimensions, particularly those aiming to address the hierarchy problem (the vast difference between the electroweak scale and the Planck scale). The left side, $M_{Pl}^2$, represents the square of the Planck mass, a fundamental constant in quantum gravity, approximately $1.22 \times 10^{19}$ GeV. The right side involves a fundamental mass scale $M_D$, which could be closer to the electroweak scale (around 1 TeV), and $R$, the radius of the compactified extra dimensions. The equation states that $M_{Pl}^2 = M_{D}^{2+n} R^n$. Here, $n$ is the number of extra spatial dimensions that are 'curled up' or compactified to a small size $R$. This equation implies that if $M_D$ is much smaller than $M_{Pl}$, then the size of these extra dimensions $R$ must be related to $M_D$ and $M_{Pl}$ in such a way that gravity becomes effectively weaker in our 4-dimensional spacetime. If $M_D$ is the fundamental scale of gravity in the higher-dimensional theory, then the apparent weakness of gravity in 4D is due to its dilution across these $n$ extra dimensions. The ADD scaling (Arkani-Hamed, Dimopoulos, Dvali) typically refers to models where $n$ can be relatively large (e.g., 2 to 7), making $R$ large enough to be potentially detectable, while the fundamental Planck scale $M_{Pl}$ in the higher-dimensional theory can be as low as $M_D$.
curled-dimensions-ec181bd3.symmetry_origin: The derivation of this relationship originates from the compactification of extra spatial dimensions in higher-dimensional theories, such as Kaluza-Klein theory or string theory. In these frameworks, the gravitational field in the higher-dimensional spacetime has a more fundamental strength. When some dimensions are compactified to a small radius $R$, the effective gravitational potential in the lower-dimensional spacetime (our observable universe) is modified. This modification leads to a relationship between the Planck mass in 4D and the fundamental Planck scale in the higher dimensions, incorporating the size of the compactified dimensions. The equation arises from considering how the gravitational action transforms from the higher-dimensional to the lower-dimensional spacetime, involving volume factors of the compactified dimensions.
curled-dimensions-ec181bd3.limits_and_boundary: As the number of extra dimensions $n$ approaches zero (i.e., we return to a 4-dimensional spacetime without compactified dimensions), the equation simplifies. If $n=0$, the equation becomes $M_{Pl}^2 = M_D^2$, implying that the Planck scale is the fundamental mass scale. As the radius of the extra dimensions $R$ becomes extremely large (approaching infinity) for a fixed $M_D$ and $n > 0$, the term $M_D^{2+n} R^n$ tends to infinity. This scenario is not physically realized in our universe, as $M_{Pl}$ is finite. Conversely, if $R$ is very small (approaching zero), and $M_D$ is kept finite, then $M_D^{2+n} R^n$ tends to zero, which would imply $M_{Pl}^2$ approaches zero, a contradiction. Therefore, for a finite $M_{Pl}$ and $M_D$, there must be a specific range for $R$ related to $n$ and the ratio $M_{Pl}/M_D$.
curled-dimensions-ec181bd3.conceptual_definition: The formula 'Curled Dimensions' relates the Planck mass squared ($M_{Pl}^2$) to a fundamental mass scale ($M_D$) in a higher-dimensional theory and the size of the extra dimensions ($R$). It suggests that gravity, which appears weak in our observable 4 spacetime dimensions, might be strong at the Planck scale in these higher dimensions. The exponent on the right-hand side depends on the number of curled or compactified extra spatial dimensions, denoted by $n$. This equation is a cornerstone in theories attempting to unify gravity with other fundamental forces by introducing extra spatial dimensions beyond the familiar three.
curled-dimensions-ec181bd3.intuitive_summary: Gravity's apparent weakness in our universe stems from its 'spreading' into extra spatial dimensions, with its true strength revealed at the Planck scale in those curled dimensions.

bulk-boundary-identity-cd00c437.conceptual_definition: The Bulk-Boundary Identity is a profound statement in theoretical physics, particularly in the context of quantum field theory and condensed matter physics, that establishes a direct equivalence between certain properties of a system's bulk (interior) and its boundary (surface or edge). It asserts that the partition function of a system, when defined in terms of its bulk degrees of freedom, can be precisely calculated by considering only the degrees of freedom localized at the boundary, under specific conditions. This identity suggests a holographic-like principle where the information contained in the higher-dimensional bulk can be encoded on a lower-dimensional boundary.
bulk-boundary-identity-cd00c437.intuitive_summary: The complex behavior of a physical system's interior can be fully understood by examining only its surface properties.

interference-maxima-condition-92e92d8e.title: Constructive Interference Condition
interference-maxima-condition-92e92d8e.interpretation: The equation $d \sin \theta = n\lambda$ relates the geometry of wave sources and the properties of the waves to the conditions for constructive interference. Here, $d$ represents the distance between two coherent wave sources, or equivalently, the spacing between slits in a diffraction grating, measured in meters (m). The angle $\theta$ is the angle between the direction of wave propagation and the direction perpendicular to the line connecting the sources (or the grating surface), measured in radians or degrees. This angle specifies the direction in which constructive interference is observed. The variable $n$ is an integer ($n = 0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \ldots$) and is known as the order of interference; $n=0$ corresponds to the central maximum, $n=1$ to the first-order maximum, and so on. Finally, $\lambda$ (lambda) is the wavelength of the waves, measured in meters (m), which characterizes the spatial period of the wave. The equation states that constructive interference occurs at specific angles $\theta$ where the path difference between waves originating from the two sources (or slits) is an integer multiple of the wavelength.
interference-maxima-condition-92e92d8e.symmetry_origin: This formula is derived from the principles of wave superposition and Huygens' principle. When waves from two coherent sources arrive at a point, their total displacement is the sum of their individual displacements. For constructive interference, the phase difference between the waves must be an integer multiple of $2\pi$ radians. This phase difference is directly related to the path difference between the waves. If the path difference is $\Delta L$, then the phase difference is $\Delta ϕ = (2\pi/\lambda) \Delta L$. For constructive interference, $\Delta ϕ = 2n\pi$. Equating these gives $(2\pi/\lambda) \Delta L = 2n\pi$, so $\Delta L = n\lambda$. In the case of two sources separated by $d$ and observed at an angle $\theta$ relative to the normal, the path difference is $\Delta L = d \sin \theta$. Substituting this into the condition for constructive interference yields the formula.
interference-maxima-condition-92e92d8e.limits_and_boundary: As the angle $\theta$ approaches $0$, $\sin \theta$ approaches $0$. This implies that for $n=0$, constructive interference occurs at $\theta=0$ (the central maximum), regardless of the separation $d$ or wavelength $\lambda$. As $d$ approaches infinity (effectively making the sources independent and non-interfering in a practical sense), the condition $d \sin \theta = n\lambda$ becomes harder to satisfy for any given $\theta$ and $n$, meaning interference effects diminish. As $\lambda$ approaches infinity, the angle $\theta$ also tends to approach $0$ for low orders $n$, indicating broad constructive interference. If $\theta$ approaches $\pi/2$ (90 degrees), $\sin \theta$ approaches 1, meaning that constructive interference can only occur if $d \ge n\lambda$. If $d < \lambda$, then only $n=0$ is possible, meaning constructive interference only occurs along the direction $\theta=0$.

square-integrable-definition-391cbf09.title: Square-Integrability Condition
square-integrable-definition-391cbf09.interpretation: In the given equation, s P(r, t)u represents the wave function of a quantum system, which depends on both position r and time t. The term |s P(r, t)|² is the probability density, indicating the likelihood of finding the particle per unit volume at position r and time t. The integral symbol s dtru represents integration over all possible spatial coordinates (volume element), often denoted as dt. The condition s dtru |s P(r, t)|² dtr < ∞ signifies that the total probability of finding the particle anywhere in the universe (the integral of the probability density over all space) must be a finite value. This finite value is normalized to 1 for a properly normalized wave function, ensuring that the particle is found with certainty somewhere.
square-integrable-definition-391cbf09.symmetry_origin: The Square-Integrability Condition arises from the probabilistic interpretation of the wave function in quantum mechanics, pioneered by Max Born. It's a consequence of the need for a consistent probabilistic framework. While not directly tied to a specific symmetry operation like spatial translation or rotation in its definition, it ensures that the system can be normalized to a total probability of one, which is a fundamental requirement for any probability distribution, and by extension, for quantum states.
square-integrable-definition-391cbf09.limits_and_boundary: As the spatial extent of the integration volume r approaches infinity, the square-integrability condition implies that the wave function s P(r, t)u must approach zero sufficiently rapidly. Specifically, |s P(r, t)|² must decay faster than 1/r³ in three dimensions for the integral to converge. If the wave function were to remain finite or grow as r → ∞, the integral of |s P(r, t)|² over all space would diverge, violating the condition and rendering the wave function non-physical. Conversely, for bounded systems or bound states, the wave function is naturally confined to a finite region, and the integral will be finite without needing extreme decay at large distances, provided the integration domain is appropriately defined.

It asserts that the integral of the squared magnitude of the wave function over all space must be finite. This condition is crucial because the squared magnitude of the wave function, |s P(r, t)|², represents the probability density of finding a particle at a particular position r and time t. If this integral were infinite, it would imply an infinite probability of finding the particle somewhere in space, which is physically nonsensical. Therefore, for a physically admissible wave function, the total probability of finding the particle in all of space must be exactly one, and consequently, the integral of the probability density must be finite.
square-integrable-definition-391cbf09.intuitive_summary: A physically valid quantum state must have a finite total probability of finding the particle somewhere in space.

vev-potential-minimum-mapping-a8b8c52b.title: VEV Potential Minimization
vev-potential-minimum-mapping-a8b8c52b.interpretation: In this formula, $v$ represents the vacuum expectation value (VEV) of the scalar field, which is the non-zero value the field settles into in its lowest energy state. The term $\mu^2$ is related to the mass parameter of the scalar field. If $\mu^2 > 0$, it corresponds to a mass-squared, and the potential has a minimum at zero field, leading to a zero VEV. However, in the context of VEV potential minimization, we are typically concerned with the case where the effective $\mu^2$ is negative, implying instability at zero field and driving the field to a non-zero minimum. $\lambda$ is a self-coupling constant for the scalar field, typically positive, which dictates the shape of the potential at large field values and ensures stability. The formula shows that a larger magnitude of the effective $\mu^2$ (i.e., a more negative $\mu^2$ for instability) leads to a larger VEV, while a stronger self-interaction $\lambda$ leads to a smaller VEV, as the field is 'pushed back' towards zero by the self-interaction.
vev-potential-minimum-mapping-a8b8c52b.symmetry_origin: This formula arises from minimizing the potential energy of a scalar field, typically described by a Lagrangian with a potential of the form $V(\phi) = \frac{1}{2}$ m^2 \phi^2 + $\frac{1}{4}$ \lambda \phi^4$. For spontaneous symmetry breaking to occur, the coefficient of the quadratic term, effectively $\mu^2$, must be negative (let's write it as $-\mu^2$ for clarity in this context, so the potential is $V(\phi) = -$\frac{1}{2}$ \mu^2 \phi^2 + $\frac{1}{4}$ \lambda \phi^4$ with $\mu^2 > 0$). The minimum of this potential is found by taking the derivative with respect to $\phi$ and setting it to zero: \frac{dV}{d\phi}$ = -\mu^2 \phi + \lambda \phi^3 = 0$. The solutions are $\phi = 0$ and $\phi^2 = $\frac{\mu^2}{\lambda}$. The non-zero solution, $\phi = \pm\sqrt{\frac{\mu^2}{\lambda}}$, represents the minimum of the potential and thus the VEV. The value of $v$ is the magnitude of this non-zero minimum, $v = \sqrt{\frac{\mu^2}{\lambda}}$. This process is called spontaneous symmetry breaking because the Lagrangian (and thus the equations of motion) is symmetric under $\phi \to -\phi$, but the vacuum state (the minimum of the potential) is not.
vev-potential-minimum-mapping-a8b8c52b.limits_and_boundary: As $\mu^2 \to 0^+$ (approaching zero from the positive side, maintaining the condition for a non-zero VEV), the VEV $v \to 0$. This implies that if the 'mass' term becomes very small, the field prefers to sit at zero, and the symmetry remains unbroken. As $\lambda \to \infty$ (strong self-interaction), the VEV $v \to 0$. A very strong self-interaction makes it energetically unfavorable for the field to deviate significantly from zero, pushing the minimum back towards $\phi = 0$. Conversely, as $\lambda \to 0^+$ (weak self-interaction), the VEV $v \to \infty$. This suggests that without sufficient self-interaction to stabilize the potential, the field could acquire an arbitrarily large VEV, indicating an unstable or ill-defined theory in this limit.

Units are Joules if the field has units of meters and is coupled linearly, or more generally, units of mass squared in particle physics contexts (e.g., (kg)^2).

If units are considered, they would be inverse powers of mass or length depending on the field's normalization.

This occurs when the potential energy of the field has a minimum at a non-zero field value, a phenomenon known as spontaneous symmetry breaking. The VEV represents the average value of the field in its ground state (vacuum).
vev-potential-minimum-mapping-a8b8c52b.intuitive_summary: This equation quantifies the strength of a scalar field's background value in its lowest energy state, determined by its self-interaction and mass-like properties.

tight-binding-sc-lattice-dispersion-d40d.title: Simple Cubic Dispersion (Tight-Binding)
tight-binding-sc-lattice-dispersion-d40d.interpretation: The formula $E(k) = E_0 - 2t [\cos(k_x a) + \cos(k_y a) + \cos(k_z a)]$ provides the energy of an electron with wavevector $k = (k_x, k_y, k_z)$ in a simple cubic lattice. The term $E_0$ represents the energy of an isolated atom, serving as a reference point. The parameter $t$, known as the hopping integral or transfer integral, quantifies the probability amplitude for an electron to move from one atomic site to an adjacent one. A larger value of $t$ implies stronger coupling between atoms and wider energy bands. The terms $\cos(k_x a)$, $\cos(k_y a)$, and $\cos(k_z a)$ account for the constructive and destructive interference of electron wavefunctions as they delocalize across the lattice in the x, y, and z directions, respectively. The lattice constant $a$ is the distance between nearest-neighbor atoms along each axis. The wavevector components $k_x, k_y, k_z$ are the crystal momentum components of the electron. The cosine functions show that the energy is maximal when $k_x = k_y = k_z = 0$ (Bloch wave with zero crystal momentum, corresponding to the atomic limit) and minimal when $k_x, k_y, k_z$ are at the Brillouin zone boundaries (e.g., $\pi/a$).
tight-binding-sc-lattice-dispersion-d40d.symmetry_origin: This formula arises from the translational symmetry of the crystal lattice. According to Bloch's theorem, the wavefunctions of electrons in a periodic potential can be written as a product of a plane wave and a function with the same periodicity as the lattice. The tight-binding model simplifies the calculation by considering only the overlap of atomic orbitals on nearest-neighbor sites. The energy dispersion relation $E(k)$ reflects the symmetry of the lattice, as the cosine terms are periodic in $k_x, k_y, k_z$ with period $2\pi/a$.
tight-binding-sc-lattice-dispersion-d40d.limits_and_boundary: In the limit of very weak hopping ($t \to 0$), the electron energy approaches the atomic energy $E(k) \to E_0$. This corresponds to electrons being strongly localized on individual atoms. At the opposite extreme, for a large hopping integral $t$, the energy bands become wide. For small wavevectors, i.e., $k_x a, k_y a, k_z a \ll 1$, the cosine terms can be approximated by $1 - \frac{(ka)^2}{2}$. Thus, $E(k) \approx E_0 - 2t [3 - \frac{1}{2}$(k_x^2 a^2 + k_y^2 a^2 + k_z^2 a^2)$] = E_0 - 6t + t a^2 (k_x^2 + k_y^2 + k_z^2) = E_0' + \frac{\hbar^2 k^2}{2m^*}$, where $E_0' = E_0 - 6t$ is a shifted atomic energy and $m^* = \frac{\hbar^2}{2ta^2}$ is the effective mass of the electron. This shows that near the center of the Brillouin zone ($k=0$), the dispersion relation becomes parabolic, characteristic of free electrons, but with an effective mass determined by the lattice properties and hopping strength.

boltzmann-h-theorem-entropy-ident-a7880f.title: Boltzmann's H-Theorem
boltzmann-h-theorem-entropy-ident-a7880f.interpretation:
The H-theorem is formally stated by the integral equation: 
$\frac{dH}{dt} = \int (f_1' f_2' - f_1 f_2) (Φ_{12} - Φ_{12}') v_{12} dΦ_{12} dΣ_1 dΣ_2 $
Here, $H$ is the Boltzmann entropy functional, which is related to the negative logarithm of the probability distribution of particle states. The integral is taken over all possible states of two interacting particles, 1 and 2. The terms $f_1$ and $f_2$ represent the distribution functions of particles 1 and 2 before a collision, and $f_1'$ and $f_2'$ represent their distribution functions after the collision. The term $(Φ_{12} - Φ_{12}')$ represents the change in the interaction potential energy during the collision, and $Ͷ_{12}$ is the relative velocity of the two particles. The equation essentially states that the rate of change of $H$ is determined by the net rate at which collisions tend to drive the system away from equilibrium. For elastic collisions, the quantity $\frac{dH}{dt}$ is shown to be less than or equal to zero, indicating a tendency towards equilibrium.
boltzmann-h-theorem-entropy-ident-a7880f.symmetry_origin: The H-theorem is derived from the principles of kinetic theory and statistical mechanics, specifically by considering the effects of binary collisions between particles in a gas. It relies on the assumption of molecular chaos (Stosszahlansatz), which states that the velocities of colliding particles are uncorrelated before the collision. While the underlying microscopic laws of physics (like Newton's laws of motion) are time-reversible, the H-theorem demonstrates an emergent macroscopic irreversibility by considering the average behavior of a large number of particles and the statistical nature of collisions.
boltzmann-h-theorem-entropy-ident-a7880f.limits_and_boundary: As time approaches infinity, the H-theorem predicts that the system will approach a state of thermodynamic equilibrium, where the distribution functions $f_i$ become independent of time, and consequently, $\frac{dH}{dt}$ approaches zero. In this equilibrium state, the H quantity reaches its minimum value, corresponding to the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution for a dilute gas. If the initial state is already in equilibrium, then $\frac{dH}{dt} = 0$ from the start.

boltzmann-h-theorem-entropy-ident-a7880f.intuitive_summary: The H-theorem shows that the randomness (or disorder) in a system of particles naturally increases over time until it reaches a state of maximum randomness, which is thermal equilibrium.

symplectic-form-identity-1-290d9ecb-60b6.title: Symplectic 2-Form Definition
symplectic-form-identity-1-290d9ecb-60b6.interpretation: The equation $\omega = \sum_{i=1}^n dp_i \wedge dq_i$ defines the canonical symplectic 2-form $\omega$ on a 2n-dimensional phase space. Here, $dq_i$ represents an infinitesimal displacement in the generalized coordinate $q_i$, and $dp_i$ represents an infinitesimal displacement in the corresponding conjugate momentum $p_i$. The wedge product $\wedge$ signifies an exterior product, forming an oriented 2-dimensional parallelogram (a 'symplectic area element') in the phase space spanned by $dp_i$ and $dq_i$. The summation over $i=1$ to $n$ indicates that the total symplectic form is the sum of these elementary area elements across all $n$ degrees of freedom of the system. This form is invariant under canonical transformations, meaning that the phase space volume (in a generalized sense defined by $\omega$) is conserved over time for Hamiltonian systems.
symplectic-form-identity-1-290d9ecb-60b6.symmetry_origin:

coulomb-force-relation-de664ace.title: Coulomb's Law Electrostatic Force Relation
coulomb-force-relation-de664ace.interpretation: The equation \textbf{F} = $\frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}$ \textbf{\hat{r}} describes the$ force experienced between two point charges. $q_1$ and $q_2$ represent the magnitudes of the two electric charges. The term $r$ is the distance between the centers of these two charges. The force is directly proportional to the product of the charges $q_1 q_2$, meaning that like charges (both positive or both negative) repel each other, resulting in a positive force magnitude in the direction away from each other, while opposite charges attract, resulting in a negative force magnitude in the direction towards each other. The force decreases with the square of the distance $r^2$, following an inverse square law. The constant \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} is Coulomb's constant, often denoted as $k_e$, which includes the permittivity of free space $\varepsilon_0$. The unit vector $\textbf{\hat{r}}$, pointing from the first charge to the second, indicates the direction of the force.
coulomb-force-relation-de664ace.symmetry_origin: Coulomb's Law is derived from experimental observations and exhibits the symmetry of a central force, meaning the force acts along the line connecting the two charges. It can also be understood as a consequence of the underlying electromagnetic field theory, specifically Maxwell's equations in a vacuum, and its relationship to the conservation of electric charge.

This formula, represented abstractly as 
\mathbf{J} → 
\mathbf{J}, is not a typical equation that quantifies a change or relationship between distinct physical quantities. Instead, it signifies an invariance or conservation principle. Specifically, it implies that the angular momentum, 
\mathbf{J}, of a system remains unchanged under certain transformations, particularly translations, provided there are no external torques acting on the system. It is a statement about the form of the physics (specifically, the laws governing motion) being the same in different inertial frames related by translation.
angular-momentum-under-translation.intuitive_summary: The angular momentum of an object or system remains constant if no external twisting forces act upon it, regardless of its translational motion.
angular-momentum-under-translation.interpretation:
The symbol 
\mathbf{J} represents the total angular momentum of a system. Angular momentum is a vector quantity that describes the rotational motion of an object or system. For a point particle of mass 
$m$ moving with velocity 
$\mathbf{v}$ at a position 
$\mathbf{r}$ relative to an origin, its angular momentum is given by 
$\mathbf{J} = \mathbf{r} × \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{r} × (m \mathbf{v})$. For a rigid body, it is the sum of the angular momenta of its constituent particles. The arrow 
$\to$ typically indicates a transformation or evolution. In this context,

$\to$

$\mathbf{J}$ is invariant under a particular transformation. When this transformation is a spatial translation, the statement implies that the physical laws governing the system's angular momentum are invariant under translation. This means that the definition and behavior of angular momentum do not change if we shift our entire coordinate system linearly through space, as long as no external torques act on the system. The invariance of angular momentum under translation is deeply connected to the conservation of linear momentum. If a system experiences no net external force, its linear momentum is conserved. Similarly, if a system experiences no net external torque, its angular momentum is conserved.
angular-momentum-under-translation.symmetry_origin:
This formula is a direct consequence of Noether's theorem, which establishes a fundamental connection between symmetries of physical laws and conserved quantities. Specifically, the invariance of the laws of physics under spatial translations (meaning the laws are the same everywhere in space) leads to the conservation of linear momentum. While not directly representing angular momentum's conservation under translation, the formula 
\mathbf{J}

complex-number-representation.title: Complex Number Representation
complex-number-representation.conceptual_definition: The formula $z = x + iy$ represents a complex number in its rectangular (or Cartesian) form. A complex number is a number that can be expressed in the form $a + bi$, where $a$ and $b$ are real numbers and $i$ is the imaginary unit, satisfying the equation $i^2 = -1$. In this specific representation, $x$ is the real part and $y$ is the imaginary part of the complex number $z$. Geometrically, a complex number can be visualized as a point or a vector in the complex plane, where the horizontal axis represents the real part and the vertical axis represents the imaginary part.
complex-number-representation.intuitive_summary: A complex number $z$ is defined by its real component $x$ and its imaginary component $y$, where $i$ is the imaginary unit such that $i^2 = -1$.
complex-number-representation.interpretation: In the equation $z = x + iy$, $z$ is the complex number itself. The term $x$ represents the real part of the complex number, which corresponds to the projection of $z$ onto the real axis in the complex plane. The term $y$ represents the imaginary part of the complex number, which is a real number that, when multiplied by the imaginary unit $i$, gives the component of $z$ along the imaginary axis. The imaginary unit $i$ is a fundamental concept in complex numbers, defined by $i^2 = -1$, and it allows for the extension of the number system beyond real numbers. This form is particularly useful for operations like addition and subtraction of complex numbers, where corresponding real and imaginary parts are combined.
complex-number-representation.symmetry_origin: The representation of complex numbers in the form $z = x + iy$ arises from the need to solve equations that have no real solutions, such as $x^2 + 1 = 0$. It can be rigorously derived from the properties of abstract algebraic fields and is closely related to the concept of vector spaces. The structure of complex numbers as a field extension of the real numbers is fundamental. In physics, complex numbers appear naturally in problems involving oscillations, waves, quantum mechanics, and electrical engineering, where they provide a concise way to handle phenomena with both amplitude and phase, or real and imaginary components representing distinct physical quantities.
complex-number-representation.limits_and_boundary: As the imaginary part $y$ approaches zero, the complex number $z$ approaches its real part $x$, i.e., $\lim_{y\to 0} (x + iy) = x$. This signifies that real numbers are a subset of complex numbers where the imaginary component is zero. There are no specific limits for $x$ or $y$ to infinity in this definition, as complex numbers can extend infinitely in both real and imaginary directions, corresponding to points moving away from the origin in the complex plane.

interaction-hamiltonian.title: Interaction Hamiltonian
interaction-hamiltonian.conceptual_definition:
The Interaction Hamiltonian, denoted as 
H_int, quantifies the energy associated with the interaction between two distinct quantum systems or degrees of freedom. It is fundamental in quantum field theory and condensed matter physics for describing how different parts of a system influence each other. This form, 
H_int = λ
A ⊗ B, is a common representation for a simple, direct interaction where the strength of the interaction is governed by a coupling constant λ, and the interaction itself is a product of operators 
A and 
B that act on separate Hilbert spaces of the two interacting systems.
interaction-hamiltonian.intuitive_summary: This formula describes how two quantum systems affect each other through a combined effect, scaled by an interaction strength.
interaction-hamiltonian.interpretation:
In the equation 
H_int = λ
A ⊗ B, 
H_int represents the Hamiltonian operator corresponding to the interaction energy between two quantum systems. The symbol ⊗ denotes the tensor product, signifying that 
A and 
B are operators acting on the Hilbert spaces of two distinct systems (or different degrees of freedom within a larger system). 
A is an operator describing some property or observable of the first system, and 
B is a corresponding operator for the second system. The product 
A ⊗ B indicates that the interaction couples these properties together. The coupling constant λ is a scalar value (which can be dimensionless or have units depending on the specific interaction) that determines the overall strength of this interaction. A larger absolute value of λ implies a stronger interaction, while λ = 0 means there is no interaction described by this Hamiltonian.
interaction-hamiltonian.symmetry_origin:
The origin of the interaction Hamiltonian is often derived from a total Hamiltonian 
H = 
H_0 + 
H_int, where 
H_0 is the Hamiltonian of the non-interacting systems. The form of 
H_int is typically motivated by physical principles such as symmetries (e.g., rotational or gauge invariance), conservation laws, or by the underlying fundamental forces being modeled (e.g., electromagnetic, weak, strong, or gravitational interactions). For instance, in quantum electrodynamics, the interaction Hamiltonian between charged particles and the electromagnetic field arises from gauge invariance.
interaction-hamiltonian.limits_and_boundary:
As the coupling constant λ approaches zero (λ → 0), the interaction Hamiltonian 
H_int also approaches zero. In this limit, the two systems become decoupled, and their dynamics are governed solely by their individual non-interacting Hamiltonians (
H → 
H_A + 
H_B). Conversely, as the magnitude of λ increases significantly, the interaction becomes dominant, and the behavior of the combined system cannot be understood by considering the systems in isolation. The operators 
A and 
B themselves might have specific limits, for example, if they represent creation or annihilation operators, their expectation values could approach zero or certain constant values depending on the state of the respective systems.

limit-negative-infinity.title: Limit to Negative Infinity
limit-negative-infinity.conceptual_definition: The expression $\theta \to -\infty$ signifies a limit process in mathematics and physics, specifically indicating that a variable or parameter, denoted by the Greek letter theta ($\theta$), is decreasing without bound, approaching negative infinity. This is not a formula that describes a physical phenomenon directly but rather a mathematical tool used to analyze the behavior of functions or systems as a particular variable tends towards infinitely negative values.
limit-negative-infinity.intuitive_summary: This notation means that the quantity represented by $\theta$ is becoming arbitrarily large in the negative direction.
limit-negative-infinity.interpretation: In this context, $\theta$ is a mathematical variable that can represent a wide range of physical quantities depending on the specific problem. For instance, $\theta$ might represent time, position, temperature, energy, or an angle. The arrow ($\to$) denotes a limit, indicating that we are examining the behavior of a system or function as $\theta$ approaches a certain value. The symbol '- $\infty$' signifies negative infinity, meaning $\theta$ is decreasing indefinitely, becoming more and more negative. For example, if $\theta$ represents time, $\theta \to -\infty$ would refer to the distant past. If $\theta$ represents energy, it would imply an infinitely low energy state, which may or may not be physically realizable. The interpretation is highly dependent on the physical system being modeled.
limit-negative-infinity.symmetry_origin: The concept of limits, including limits to negative infinity, originates from calculus, developed by mathematicians such as Isaac Newton and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz. It is a fundamental tool for understanding continuity, derivatives, and integrals. In physics, limits are crucial for defining concepts like asymptotic behavior, the behavior of systems at extreme conditions (e.g., very large distances, very long times, or very low temperatures), and for analyzing phase transitions and singularities. The mathematical framework of limits provides a rigorous way to handle infinitely small or infinitely large quantities, which often appear in physical models.
limit-negative-infinity.limits_and_boundary: As a variable $\theta$ approaches negative infinity ($\theta \to -\infty$), the behavior of a function or physical system dependent on $\theta$ can exhibit specific characteristics. This might include approaching a constant asymptotic value, diverging to positive or negative infinity, or exhibiting oscillatory behavior. For example, in some systems, as time $t \to -\infty$, a quantity might approach a steady-state value, indicating a historical equilibrium. Conversely, other quantities might diverge, implying an unstable or unbounded historical trajectory. The specific outcome depends entirely on the mathematical form of the function or the physical laws governing the system.

$\\theta$.description: Represents a mathematical variable or parameter that is decreasing without bound, tending towards negative infinity. The physical meaning of $\theta$ is context-dependent and could represent time, position, energy, temperature, or any other quantity relevant to the physical model being analyzed.

sum-probabilities-one.title: Sum of probabilities is one
sum-probabilities-one.conceptual_definition: The formula $\sum P_i = 1$ is a fundamental axiom in probability theory and quantum mechanics, stating that the sum of the probabilities of all possible mutually exclusive outcomes of an event or a set of states must equal one. This signifies that the set of all possible outcomes is exhaustive; one of these outcomes is guaranteed to occur.
sum-probabilities-one.intuitive_summary: The probability of *something* happening, considering all possibilities, is always 100%.
sum-probabilities-one.interpretation: In this equation, $P_i$ represents the probability of the $i$-th possible outcome or state. The index $i$ runs over all distinct and mutually exclusive possibilities. For instance, if we are considering the outcome of a single die roll, the possible outcomes are $i = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6$, and the probability of rolling any specific number is $P_i = 1/6$. The summation symbol, $\sum$, indicates that we add up the probabilities of all these individual outcomes. Therefore, $\sum P_i = P_1 + P_2 + \dots + P_6 = 1/6 + 1/6 + 1/6 + 1/6 + 1/6 + 1/6 = 1$. The total probability of 1 signifies that one of these outcomes is certain to occur when the experiment is performed. This principle applies broadly, from classical probability to the normalization of wave functions in quantum mechanics where the integral of the probability density over all space must be 1.
sum-probabilities-one.symmetry_origin: This principle originates from the fundamental axioms of probability theory, specifically the axiom that the probability of the sample space (the set of all possible outcomes) is 1. It reflects the certainty that in any given experiment or observation, one of the defined possible outcomes will indeed materialize. In quantum mechanics, this equation serves as a normalization condition for the state vector or wave function, ensuring that the total probability of finding the particle somewhere in space is unity.
sum-probabilities-one.limits_and_boundary: This equation is not typically analyzed in terms of limits approaching zero or infinity for the sum itself, as the sum is a fixed value of 1. However, individual probabilities $P_i$ can approach zero (for very unlikely events) or one (for certain events). If there were only one possible outcome, its probability would be 1, and the sum would trivially be 1. If there were an infinite number of possible outcomes, each with an infinitesimally small probability, their sum must still converge to 1.

$\\sum$.description: The mathematical operator indicating the sum of a sequence of terms. In this context, it sums the probabilities of all possible mutually exclusive outcomes.

warped-metric-randall-sundrum.title: Warped Metric (Randall-Sundrum)
warped-metric-randall-sundrum.conceptual_definition: The Warped Metric (Randall-Sundrum) formula describes a specific type of spacetime geometry used in braneworld scenarios, particularly the Randall-Sundrum models. In these models, our observable universe is envisioned as a 3-dimensional 'brane' embedded in a higher-dimensional 'bulk' spacetime. This metric quantifies how distances and time intervals are measured within this higher-dimensional space, taking into account the exponential warping of spacetime, which is crucial for understanding phenomena like the hierarchy problem. The metric effectively 'warps' the extra dimension, causing gravity to be much weaker on our brane compared to the higher-dimensional Planck scale.
warped-metric-randall-sundrum.intuitive_summary: This formula describes a curved spacetime where the curvature depends exponentially on a fifth coordinate, effectively localizing matter and forces to a lower-dimensional brane within a higher-dimensional space.
warped-metric-randall-sundrum.interpretation: The equation defines the infinitesimal spacetime interval, denoted by $ds^2$. It is composed of two parts. The first part, $\eta_{\mu\nu} dx^\mu dx^^\nu$, represents the Minkowski metric in four spacetime dimensions (3 spatial + 1 time), indicating the 'flat' nature of the spacetime in the absence of warping. This is multiplied by an exponential factor, $e^{-2k|y|}$, which signifies the warping of spacetime. Here, $k$ is a constant related to the curvature of the bulk spacetime, and $y$ is the coordinate along the extra dimension. The term $|y|$ ensures that the warping is symmetric around $y=0$. This exponential factor means that as one moves away from the brane (i.e., as $|y|$ increases), the effective spacetime interval in the four dimensions shrinks, and thus gravity appears weaker. The second term, $dy^2$, represents the proper distance element in the extra dimension. In Randall-Sundrum models, matter and Standard Model fields are confined to a 3-brane, while gravity can propagate in the bulk.
warped-metric-randall-sundrum.symmetry_origin: This metric is derived from the Einstein Field Equations under specific assumptions for the stress-energy tensor and boundary conditions in a higher-dimensional spacetime. It embodies a particular form of coordinate invariance, where the physical observables are independent of the choice of coordinates. The exponential warping is a solution to Einstein's equations in a space with a specific vacuum energy (cosmological constant) in the bulk, and it is engineered to keep Standard Model particles localized on the brane while allowing gravity to propagate in the extra dimension.
warped-metric-randall-sundrum.limits_and_boundary: As $|y|$ approaches 0 (i.e., at the location of the brane), the exponential factor $e^{-2k|y|}$ approaches 1. In this limit, the metric reduces to $ds^2 = \eta_{\mu\nu} dx^\mu dx^\nu + dy^2$. If we consider only the four-dimensional part, it becomes the standard Minkowski metric of flat spacetime. As $|y|$ approaches infinity, the exponential factor $e^{-2k|y|}$ approaches 0. This means that the four-dimensional part of the spacetime interval effectively vanishes, indicating that phenomena propagating in these dimensions become infinitely suppressed. This is how gravity is localized to the brane and appears weak far away from it.

constant-proper-acceleration-relation.title: Constant proper acceleration relation
constant-proper-acceleration-relation.conceptual_definition: The formula relates the spatial distance and time elapsed for an object undergoing constant proper acceleration, often visualized in the context of spacetime geometry. It is derived from the worldline of such an object in Minkowski spacetime and has implications in special relativity, particularly concerning hyperbolic motion.
constant-proper-acceleration-relation.intuitive_summary: This equation describes a constant 'hyperbolic distance' in spacetime for an object experiencing continuous acceleration.
constant-proper-acceleration-relation.interpretation:

The quantity $1/a^2$ is the inverse square of the proper acceleration, $a$, which is the acceleration experienced by an observer co-moving with the object. constant-proper-acceleration-relation.symmetry_origin: This equation is fundamentally related to the geometry of Minkowski spacetime and the concept of hyperbolic motion in special relativity. The symmetry arises from the invariance of the spacetime interval. For hyperbolic motion, the worldline of an object is a hyperbola in spacetime. The equation can be seen as a statement about the parameters defining this hyperbola in a specific coordinate system, related to the constant proper acceleration.

tangent-vector-curve.title: Tangent vector to a curve
tangent-vector-curve.conceptual_definition: The tangent vector to a curve in spacetime, represented by the equation $ k^\mu = dx^\mu/d\lambda $, is a fundamental concept in differential geometry and general relativity. It describes the instantaneous direction and rate of change of a curve parameterized by $ \lambda $. In the context of physics, a curve in spacetime often represents the worldline of a particle or a light ray. The tangent vector then signifies the velocity or the direction of propagation of that entity at a specific point along its path. The index $ \mu $ indicates that this is a four-vector, meaning it has components in each of the four spacetime dimensions (typically one time dimension and three spatial dimensions).
tangent-vector-curve.intuitive_summary: This equation defines the velocity four-vector of a particle or light ray as the rate of change of its spacetime position with respect to a parameter along its path.
tangent-vector-curve.interpretation: The equation $ k^\mu = dx^\mu/d\lambda $ describes the tangent vector $ k^\mu $ to a curve in spacetime. The curve is defined by its spacetime coordinates $ x^\mu $, which are functions of a parameter $ \lambda $. The parameter $ \lambda $ is often chosen to have a specific physical meaning; for instance, it can be proper time for massive particles or an affine parameter for light rays. The equation states that each component of the tangent vector $ k^\mu $ is the derivative of the corresponding spacetime coordinate $ x^\mu $ with respect to this parameter $ \lambda $. Therefore, $ k^\mu $ represents the four-velocity of a particle if $ \lambda $ is the proper time, or the four-momentum if $ \lambda $ is scaled appropriately. The derivative $ dx^\mu/d\lambda $ essentially measures how much each spacetime coordinate changes for a unit change in $ \lambda $, thus defining the direction and magnitude of the curve's instantaneous change in spacetime. The index $ \mu $ takes values 0, 1, 2, 3, corresponding to time and the three spatial dimensions, making $ k^\mu $ a four-vector.
tangent-vector-curve.symmetry_origin: This formula is derived from the fundamental principles of differential geometry, specifically the definition of a tangent vector to a parameterized curve. In physics, its origin lies in describing the motion of objects in spacetime. It is coordinate-independent in the sense that while the components of $ x^\mu $ and $ k^\mu $ depend on the chosen coordinate system, the geometric object represented by the tangent vector (and its relation to the curve) is invariant. This aligns with the principle of general covariance in relativity, which states that physical laws should take the same form in all coordinate systems.
tangent-vector-curve.limits_and_boundary: As the parameter $ \lambda $ approaches a specific value, the tangent vector $ k^\mu $ represents the instantaneous velocity at that point on the curve. If the parameter $ \lambda $ represents proper time $ \tau $, and the particle is at rest, its spatial components of $ dx^\mu/d\tau $ would be zero, with only the time component being non-zero (related to the rate of time flow). If $ \lambda $ is an affine parameter for a light ray, $ d x^\mu/d\lambda $ would represent the direction of propagation of the light, and its magnitude (in Minkowski spacetime) would be zero.

poisson-equation-greens-function-dirichl.title: Solution to Poisson's equation using Green's function (with Dirichlet boundary conditions)
poisson-equation-greens-function-dirichl.equation: \Phi(\mathbf{r}) = \frac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \int_V \rho(\mathbf{r}') G_D(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}') d^3\mathbf{r}' - \frac{1}{4\pi}\oint_{\partial V} g(\mathbf{r}') \frac{\partial G_D(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{r}')}{\partial n'} da'
poisson-equation-greens-function-dirichl.conceptual_definition: This formula provides a general solution for Poisson's equation, ∇²Φ(ᵗ) = -ρ(ᵗ)/ε₀, in a given volume ℘ under Dirichlet boundary conditions. It expresses the potential Φ(ᵗ) at a point ᵗ) as a superposition of contributions from the charge distribution ρ(ᵗ')) within the volume and from the boundary conditions specified on the surface ∂℘. The method leverages the Green's function, denoted as ᵊ_D(ᵗ, ᵗ'), which is the solution to Poisson's equation with a point source and satisfies the specified boundary conditions.
poisson-equation-greens-function-dirichl.intuitive_summary: The total electric potential at a point is the sum of contributions from all charges within a region and the influence of potentials or their normal derivatives on the region's boundary.
poisson-equation-greens-function-dirichl.interpretation: The equation Φ(ᵗ) = ⅒⁴πε₀⁵$\delta$ \int_℘ ρ(ᵗ')) ᵊ_D(ᵗ, ᵗ')) d³ᵗ') - ⅒⁴π⁵$\delta$ \int_{∂℘} g(ᵗ')) ∂ᵊ_D(ᵗ, ᵗ')/∂n') da') describes the electric potential Φ(ᵗ) (in Volts) at a position ᵗ) within a volume ℘. The first term represents the contribution from the charge density ρ(ᵗ')) (in Coulombs per cubic meter, C/m³) located at position ᵗ') within the volume ℘. This integral is weighted by the Green's function ᵊ_D(ᵗ, ᵗ'), which accounts for the influence of the charge at ᵗ') on the potential at ᵗ), considering the geometry and boundary conditions. The constant ε₀ is the permittivity of free space (in Farads per meter, F/m). The second term accounts for the influence of the boundary conditions on the surface ∂℘ of the volume. Here, ᵊ_D(ᵗ, ᵗ') is the Green's function evaluated at the boundary point ᵗ'), and its normal derivative ∂ᵊ_D(ᵗ, ᵗ')/∂n' (with ∂n' being the outward normal derivative) represents the rate of change of the Green's function normal to the surface. This term is weighted by a function ᵊ(ᵗ')) which is related to the boundary potential or its normal derivative, depending on how the Green's function is defined and the specific boundary conditions (e.g., for Dirichlet conditions, ᵊ(ᵗ')) would be related to the specified potential on the boundary). This integral is over the surface area ∂℘. This equation is a manifestation of the superposition principle for linear differential equations like Poisson's equation.
poisson-equation-greens-function-dirichl.symmetry_origin: This solution originates from the mathematical technique of using Green's functions to solve inhomogeneous linear partial differential equations. The Green's function itself is the response of the system to a point source (a Dirac delta function) and satisfies the homogeneous equation with specific boundary conditions. The derivation relies on the linearity of Poisson's equation and the properties of integral equations, particularly the symmetry of the Green's function in certain physical contexts (though not always explicit in the formula itself for a general ᵊ_D) and the application of Green's theorem.
poisson-equation-greens-function-dirichl.limits_and_boundary: In the limit where the volume ℘ becomes infinitely large and the boundary ∂℘ recedes to infinity, the second integral term typically vanishes if the Green's function decays appropriately at infinity (e.g., for the free-space Green's function, ᵊ_D(ᵗ, ᵗ') → 0 as |ᵗ| → ∞). In this scenario, the potential is solely determined by the total charge distribution within the infinite volume. Conversely, if the charge density ρ(ᵗ') is zero everywhere within the volume (℘), the potential Φ(ᵗ) is entirely determined by the boundary conditions through the surface integral term.

galilean-time-transformation-37b7b73f.title: Galilean Time Transformation
galilean-time-transformation-37b7b73f.description: This equation states that time is absolute and flows uniformly for all inertial observers in Galilean mechanics.
galilean-time-transformation-37b7b73f.conceptual_definition: In the framework of Galilean relativity, time is considered an independent parameter that is universal and absolute. This means that the measurement of a time interval between two events is the same for all inertial observers, regardless of their relative motion. There is no concept of time dilation or length contraction in this classical model of spacetime.
galilean-time-transformation-37b7b73f.interpretation: The equation \(t' = t\) signifies that time itself is not affected by changes in an observer's inertial reference frame. If an event occurs at time \(t\) in one inertial frame, it occurs at the same time \(t'\) in another inertial frame moving at a constant velocity relative to the first. This implies a universal clock that ticks identically for everyone, forming the basis of classical mechanics where simultaneity is absolute.
galilean-time-transformation-37b7b73f.limits_and_boundary: This equation is valid only within the classical regime where relative velocities between observers are much smaller than the speed of light (\(v \ll c\)). It breaks down at relativistic speeds, where time dilation effects become significant and are described by the Lorentz transformations. It assumes a flat, Euclidean spacetime.
galilean-time-transformation-37b7b73f.symmetry_origin: The absolute nature of time in Galilean mechanics is a direct consequence of the underlying assumption of a universal, independent time parameter. This implies a symmetry under Galilean boosts, where the time coordinate remains invariant. It is related to the conservation of energy and momentum in a system, as the time coordinate is decoupled from spatial coordinates in this transformation.

velocity-acceleration-orthogonality-cond.title: Velocity-Acceleration Orthogonality Condition
velocity-acceleration-orthogonality-cond.description: This equation states that the velocity vector and the acceleration vector of an object are perpendicular to each other. It signifies motion at a constant speed.
velocity-acceleration-orthogonality-cond.conceptual_definition: In vector calculus, the dot product of two non-zero vectors being zero signifies that the vectors are orthogonal. For an object in motion, this means its instantaneous velocity and instantaneous acceleration are at right angles. This condition specifically implies that the magnitude of the velocity (speed) is constant.
velocity-acceleration-orthogonality-cond.interpretation: When $\mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{a} = 0$, the acceleration has no component along the direction of motion. This means the acceleration is solely responsible for changing the direction of the velocity vector, not its magnitude. Consequently, the object moves with a constant speed, even though its direction of motion might be continuously changing, as seen in uniform circular motion where centripetal acceleration is always perpendicular to velocity.
velocity-acceleration-orthogonality-cond.limits_and_boundary: This condition applies specifically to motion where the speed of the object is constant. It does not hold for motion where the speed is changing (e.g., linear acceleration or deceleration). It is a specific kinematic condition rather than a universal law.
velocity-acceleration-orthogonality-cond.symmetry_origin: This condition is a direct consequence of the invariance of the magnitude of the velocity vector. It reflects a specific type of motion where the energy associated with translational motion remains constant, often related to forces that do no work on the object.
